related_resources.reason: Special relativity, reference frames, proper time, intervals and energy.
Relativistic GPS satellite clock shift: -7, +45, +38 microseconds per day.
Hafele–Keating clocks, gravitational and speed-dependent time comparisons.

historical_claims.anchor: But in the setting of special relativity, the fixed vacuum speed of light demands a change in our ideas about space and time.
At sixty percent of the speed of light, the square is zero point three six, the square root is zero point eight, and gamma is one point two five.
For the train moving at sixty percent of light speed, a one-hundred-meter proper length corresponds to eighty meters in the platform frame.
Neglecting the finite duration of turnaround, the stay-at-home clock registers eight years between departure and reunion.
In the early 1970s, Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating transported atomic clocks aboard commercial aircraft and compared them with clocks that stayed on the ground.
Their orbital speeds lead to a special-relativistic contribution of roughly seven microseconds per day slower than Earthbound clocks.
Their higher gravitational potential produces a gravitational contribution of roughly forty-five microseconds per day faster.
Thirty-eight millionths of a second sounds negligible.

description: Introduces relativity through clock comparisons, space-time measurements, and the effects of motion and gravity on elapsed time.
